alt: NASA CERES map of reflected shortwave radiation averaged over 2000–2015, with a 0–385 W m⁻² colour scale.
caption: This CERES observation maps reflected sunlight. Solar absorption by the Earth system is the incoming shortwave energy minus this reflected component; the image measures reflection rather than absorption directly.

credit: Aravind Sivaraj / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: A hand pump used to draw groundwater at Perambalur, India.
caption: Groundwater hand pump at Perambalur, India. Abstraction removes water from an aquifer; pumping may lower the water level around a well, which is measured below ground.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Tropical forest at Bodiman, Cameroon. This is a landscape example for tropical rainforest climate; an Af classification is determined from long-term monthly temperature and rainfall, not from vegetation alone.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: The Hawaiian volcanic islands stretch across the Pacific beneath scattered white clouds in an ISS photograph.
caption: Hawaii from the ISS. The volcanic chain records Pacific plate motion relative to a long-lived hotspot; the youngest main island is at the southeast end.

credit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Satellite image of the parallel folded ridges of the Appalachian Mountains and Chesapeake Bay.
caption: NASA Terra MODIS, 15 September 2023. Appalachian ridges and valleys across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania preserve the structure of an ancient mountain belt.

credit: Peter Pearson / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Grey London Clay exposed below yellow-brown Red Crag in the sea cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex.
caption: London Clay forms the lower part of the Naze cliffs. Clay-rich beds commonly transmit groundwater slowly and can act as aquitards; the cliff exposes the material, while permeability is established by testing.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Green crystalline mantle peridotite enclosed by darker volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona.
caption: Mantle peridotite enclosed in volcanic host rock at Peridot Mesa, Arizona. It is physical evidence of rock from the upper mantle. The mantle is predominantly solid; local partial melting is not a global magma ocean.

credit: Jan Nyssen, Sander Tielens, Tesfamichael Gebreyohannes, Tigist Araya, Kassa Teka, Johan Van de Wauw, Karen Degeyndt, Katrien Descheemaeker, Kassa Amare, Mitiku Haile, Amanuel Zenebe, Neil Munro, Kristine Walraevens, Kindeya Gebrehiwot, Jean Poesen, Amaury Frankl, Alemtsehay Tsegay, Jozef Deckers / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Field photographs of red and black soils at different positions on the Addi Selam hillslope in Ethiopia.
caption: Addi Selam, Ethiopia: published field photographs compare red and black soils along a hillslope. Slope position changes drainage and material movement.

credit: Denali National Park and Preserve / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Glacier ice occupies a steep-sided mountain basin in Denali National Park, Alaska.
caption: A mountain basin occupied by glacier ice in the Muldrow Glacier area, Denali. A basin is a low area bounded by higher ground; drainage basins are defined by the area contributing water to an outlet.

credit: Ustill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · resized
alt: A broad, grassy former river valley near Blumberg, now drained by the much smaller Aitrach.
caption: The Aitrach valley preserves the former route of the Feldberg Danube. Capture by the Wutach diverted its large upstream flow towards the Rhine, leaving the small Aitrach in an oversized valley. The channel itself is difficult to distinguish in this landscape view.

credit: National Weather Service / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

credit: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag) / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 · resized
alt: Tall orange sand dunes under a clear sky at Sossusvlei, Namibia.
caption: Sossusvlei dunes, Namib Desert. Wind transports loose sand by surface creep and saltation; the dunes record accumulated transport rather than individual grain paths.

credit: Lysippos / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Rock contact exposed along the Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag in northwest Scotland.
caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag juxtaposes rocks with different geological histories. Such field contacts help reconstruct the Caledonian mountain belt and its crustal terranes; boundaries between terranes need regional evidence as well as one outcrop.

credit: Wilson44691 / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Fossilised Ogyopsis klotzi trilobite preserved in dark shale.
caption: Ogyopsis klotzi from the Middle Cambrian Mount Stephen Trilobite Beds, Canada. Fossils help correlate and interpret ancient sedimentary rocks.

credit: Lauren Dauphin / NASA Earth Observatory · Aqua MODIS / EOSDIS · public domain · resized
alt: Green phytoplankton and sediment-rich water off Mauritania's desert coast, observed by Aqua MODIS.
caption: Aqua MODIS, 5 May 2020. Upwelling in the Canary Current system supplies nutrients off Mauritania. The visible green water contains phytoplankton and sediment; it is not a temperature map.

credit: Manfred Heyde / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Green fields and wooded valleys on Exmoor in North Devon.
caption: Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape within the Cfb oceanic climate region. Köppen classes use long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, not the weather on the day of the photograph.

credit: Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A pale specimen of kaolinite from Ixtassou, France.
caption: Kaolinite from Ixtassou, France, is a clay mineral. Clay as a soil texture means particles smaller than 0.002 mm; mineral identity and particle size are different properties.

credit: James T M Towill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Weather instruments inside the enclosure at Charterhall in the Scottish Borders.
caption: Charterhall weather station, Scotland. Standardised instruments measure local conditions; climate describes their statistics over many years.

credit: NASA Blue Marble / Mdf (projection) · public domain · via Wikimedia Commons · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery displayed in the curved-outline Robinson projection.
caption: NASA satellite imagery in Robinson projection. This compromise projection balances several distortions; it preserves neither all areas nor all local angles.

credit: Jim D. Griggs, HVO (USGS) staff photographer[1][2] / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An arching orange lava fountain erupts from a vent on Kīlauea amid dark cooling lava.
caption: Lava fountains at Kīlauea show magma reaching the surface through a volcanic vent. Its subsurface conduit is inferred from geophysical observations and eruptive behaviour, not visible through the rock.

credit: Mdf / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NASA Blue Marble imagery in Mercator projection, with strongly enlarged high-latitude regions.
caption: NASA Blue Marble imagery reprojected by Mdf into Mercator. Local angles are preserved, area grows towards the poles, and a constant-bearing route plots as a straight line.

credit: NOAA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: NOAA bathymetry map of the South Atlantic showing continental shelves and the mid-ocean ridge.
caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Colour represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

credit: Richard Mortel / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Open grassland and sparsely vegetated hills near Jargalant, northern Mongolia.
caption: Steppe near Jargalant, Mongolia, far from a moderating ocean. Continental interiors often have larger annual temperature ranges; a weather station's long-term record is needed to measure that range.

credit: United States Department of the Interior Geological Survey / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: USGS topographic map of Mount Rainier with contours, glaciers and named summits.
caption: USGS Mount Rainier topographic sheet, published in 1971. Contours connect equal elevations; close spacing marks steep slopes.

credit: NASA image courtesy Jeff Schmaltz, LANCE MODIS Rapid Response. Caption by Michon Scott. / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Cyclone Evan's spiral cloud bands cross the islands of Fiji in a NASA satellite image.
caption: Aqua MODIS observed Cyclone Evan near Fiji on 16 December 2012. Its cloud bands spiral around the centre; a mathematical logarithmic spiral is an approximation, not a measured exact fit.

credit: NASA / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Snow-covered Himalayan peaks and valleys photographed from the International Space Station.
caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: crust shortened and thickened as India collided with Eurasia.

credit: Unidentified NOAA photographer / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: A Deep SOLO profiling float is lowered from the research vessel Kaʻimikai-O-Kanaloa in 2018.
caption: NOAA Deep SOLO deployment, 2018. Profiling floats measure ocean temperature and salinity at depth, helping scientists study density structure and deep circulation. The ocean conveyor is a simplified description of a complex circulation.

credit: Sidoine MBOGNI / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Dense green tropical forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon.
caption: Forest canopy at Bodiman, Cameroon. Leaves intercept rain and absorb light for photosynthesis; the photograph shows the living store, not the invisible molecular reactions.

credit: Alvesgaspar / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.5 · resized
alt: A breaking wave curls and foams along the coast at Porto Covo, Portugal.
caption: A breaking wave at Porto Covo, Portugal. In shallow water a wave slows and steepens; its crest eventually breaks.

credit: Mark Reid, USGS / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: An aerial view of the Oso landslide's bare source scar, debris path and deposits across the valley.
caption: Oso, Washington, 2014: an aerial photograph of the landslide source, travel path and deposit. The displaced material crossed the valley floor.

credit: Chip Clark / Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History · CC0 · resized
alt: Metallic black octahedral magnetite crystals on rock, Smithsonian specimen B10614 from Binnental, Switzerland.
caption: Magnetite, photographed in the Smithsonian collection. Pure magnetite loses its spontaneous magnetic ordering near 580 °C, its Curie temperature. This specimen photograph shows the mineral, not a temperature measurement.

credit: Kyle Hawton / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Glen Canyon Dam holds back Lake Powell above a narrow river gorge.
caption: Glen Canyon Dam and Lake Powell, Arizona. Reservoir storage and controlled releases alter the timing and size of flows downstream.

alt: Meteosat view of Earth's day–night boundary on the December solstice, with more of the Southern Hemisphere in daylight.
caption: Meteosat-9 observed this day–night boundary on 21 December 2010. Earth's tilted axis puts the subsolar point south of the equator and gives southern latitudes longer days. Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equatorial plane; the tilt of the boundary is observational evidence, not an angle scale.

Declination is the Sun's angle north or south of the equatorial plane; the tilt of the boundary is observational evidence, not an angle scale.

credit: PawełS / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: Younger gently dipping red sandstone overlies steep grey beds at Siccar Point, Scotland.
caption: The unconformity at Siccar Point records a gap of many millions of years. Ma means million years ago and ka means thousand years ago; those intervals are inferred from geological evidence, not from the photograph alone.

caption: NOAA CTD water sampling. Temperature and salinity observations constrain water density and help identify deep-water masses such as North Atlantic Deep Water. The instrument photo does not show the global circulation itself.

caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation.

caption: GOES-East cloud observations over the Americas, 22 April 2014. Tropical cloud bands and midlatitude systems provide evidence of atmospheric circulation. The three-cell pattern is a long-term zonal average, not three fixed cloud rings in this single image.

caption: SDO's time sequence of the 2012 Venus transit. Such alignments require the planet to be near an orbital node. Historical transit timing helped determine the Earth–Sun distance, now represented by the precisely defined astronomical unit.

caption: NASA CERES, April 2015. Satellite observations map outgoing thermal radiation at the top of the atmosphere in W m⁻²; colder cloud tops generally emit less than warm clear-sky regions.

caption: NASA satellite imagery reprojected by Strebe into Mollweide. This equal-area projection preserves relative areas but distorts shapes; the ocean has been lightened for legibility.

credit: James St. John / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 · resized
alt: Rounded potholes cut into dark bedrock beside flowing water in the Presque Isle River, Michigan.
caption: Presque Isle River, Michigan. Sediment circulating in eddies abrades the bedrock, enlarging these potholes.

credit: Giles Laurent / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized
alt: The Aletsch Glacier curves through a steep Alpine valley, with dark medial moraines running along its surface.
caption: The Aletsch Glacier stores water on land. Melting land ice adds water to the ocean and contributes to eustatic sea-level rise; this photograph alone does not quantify a global sea-level change.

credit: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand / Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · resized
alt: Wisps of low fog rise above a calm lake on a frosty morning, with trees reflected in the water.
caption: Evaporation fog over a lake. Water vapour mixes into colder air and condenses into droplets; invisible vapour itself cannot be photographed.

alt: A broad spiral of white clouds over the Pacific northeast of Japan.
caption: MODIS observed this extratropical cyclone northeast of Japan on 22 February 2012. Cloud bands trace the low-pressure circulation.

alt: A streamflow-gauging station beside Huey Creek in Antarctica's rocky McMurdo Dry Valleys.
caption: USGS stream-gauging station at Huey Creek, Antarctica. A time series from a gauge reveals a hydrograph's rising limb, peak and falling limb. Lag time compares rainfall timing with the discharge peak; it is not a distance along the river.

caption: NASA CERES observations, 2000–2015 mean. Colours show sunlight reflected by the Earth system in W m⁻². This is outgoing shortwave flux, not incoming solar irradiance or albedo itself.

credit: Kevin M. Gill / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0 · resized
alt: A rounded specimen of augen gneiss with pale mineral eyes enclosed in dark, folded bands.
caption: Augen gneiss: deformation and metamorphism organise minerals into bands around larger crystals. Rock-cycle pathways need not follow one fixed loop.

credit: Edal Anton Lefterov / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 · resized
alt: Brown coal exposed at Chukurovo in Bulgaria.
caption: Lignite at Chukurovo, Bulgaria. This fossil fuel formed from buried plant material; combustion transfers its stored carbon to the atmosphere.

Four figures identify a 1 km square; six identify a 100 m square. This reduced 1:250,000 sheet illustrates the system; use a detailed map for precise references.

caption: NOAA South Atlantic bathymetry. Colour represents seafloor depth, revealing continental margins, abyssal basins and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

alt: An orange windsock extends above a field beside the path to Green Lane Farm.
caption: A field windsock shows near-surface wind direction. Drag from terrain and vegetation slows flow and can turn it across isobars; the pressure gradient itself is not measured by a windsock.

credit: Chris Andrews / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: Angular rock blocks cover the summit of Foel Fras in Wales.
caption: Blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales. Physical weathering breaks bedrock into angular fragments without changing its minerals.

alt: Saturn and its broad rings in a natural-colour mosaic photographed by the Cassini spacecraft.
caption: Cassini, 6 October 2004: a natural-colour mosaic of Saturn and its rings. The rings are a thin disc of orbiting particles.

alt: Swarm-derived maps compare Earth's magnetic field intensity in 2014 and 2025, with a nanoTesla scale.
caption: Swarm satellite observations constrain Earth's magnetic field. Its main source is the moving, conducting liquid outer core, not a permanent bar magnet; the solid inner core and the core's temperature are inferred from other evidence too.

alt: Four NOAA surface analysis charts show pressure contours and weather fronts during a North American storm.
caption: NOAA surface analyses during a late-February 2022 storm. Isobars join equal pressure; front symbols identify analysed boundaries between air masses.

credit: Richard Sutcliffe / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 · resized
alt: A low grassy coastal terrace below an older cliff near Northbank.
caption: A raised beach at Northbank records former relative sea level. Relative sea level can change through land motion, including glacial rebound, and through eustatic change in global ocean level; the photograph alone cannot separate their contributions.

credit: Plorpy2 / Wikimedia Commons · CC0 · resized
alt: Photographs of clay samples comparing grey reduced material and oxidised reddish material.
caption: Real clay samples showing contrasting redox conditions. Prolonged saturation restricts oxygen, often producing grey gley colours; oxidation can produce reddish mottles.

alt: A spherical sundial with hour markings and a movable gnomon at Green's Windmill, Nottingham.

caption: Library of Congress: Hondius terrestrial globe gores, reissued by Giuseppe di Rossi in 1615. This is a scan of a real cartographic object; the tapered paper strips were designed to fit a spherical globe. Its historical geography is not a modern reference map.

alt: A groyne extends across the beach at Tallebudgera Creek on Australia's Gold Coast.
caption: Tallebudgera Creek, Gold Coast, in the 1980s. A groyne interrupts sediment movement along a beach and can change sediment supply farther down-drift.

caption: NOAA multibeam survey of an Arctic seamount. A seamount is a submarine mountain; a guyot is the flat-topped subtype. Surveyed topography, rather than colour alone, is needed to distinguish them.

alt: False-colour MODIS brightness-temperature image showing the Gulf Stream and warm eddies in the North Atlantic.
caption: MODIS observations trace warm Gulf Stream water in the western North Atlantic. The Gulf Stream is one part of the basin-scale subtropical gyre; a single current image does not show the whole circulation.

alt: The Wutach flows through a narrow, wooded gorge below exposed rock walls in the Black Forest.
caption: Wutach Gorge, Germany. Capture diverted drainage from the Danube system towards the Rhine; subsequent incision cut this gorge.

alt: The muddy Ucayali River winds through forest in Peru, with abandoned bends beside the active channel.
caption: Meanders on Peru's Ucayali River from the ISS. Bend circulation helps redistribute sediment across the channel. A long profile instead plots bed elevation downstream and requires measured heights; this plan view is not that profile.

alt: Rounded hills and fields around the Vale of Edale, viewed from Grindslow Knoll.
caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District, England. A landscape photograph shows local relief, ridges and valley slopes.
